title: How Burning Man Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Burning Man, the week-long festival held in the Black Rock Desert of Nevada, where volunteers build a temporary city (Black Rock City) that is dismantled afterward with no trace left. They cover its origins in 1986 on Baker Beach in San Francisco as an effigy burning, its move to the desert, the Bureau of Land Management relationship, the ten principles (added officially in 2004) such as radical self-expression, radical inclusion, gifting, leave no trace, and participation, the annual art themes, the ticket sales cap of around 50,000 and sliding-scale pricing, the city's layout around the Man statue, practical survival tips (water, dust, cold nights, fire rules, no driving on the playa), safety and adult-content concerns, and a sidebar on the Source Family cult and Polyphonic Spree. The episode ends with listener mail correcting an earlier segment on the FDA's blood donation ban for men who have sex with men.

segments.title: Opening banter and whether to attend Burning Man
segments.summary: Hosts joke about passing the conk and ask whether they would attend Burning Man; neither wants to go, though both find it interesting.

segments.title: What Burning Man is and the Black Rock City concept
segments.summary: Burning Man is a week-long festival in the Black Rock Desert of Nevada where a temporary planned city is built and then taken down, with everything not removed burned. Participants are called burners; volunteers build and dismantle the city.

segments.title: Annual art themes and theme camps
segments.summary: Hosts describe the yearly art theme (2013 is a cargo cult theme; earlier themes included Metropolis, Evolution, American Dream, Hope and Fear, and the Green Man) and how burners create theme camps or large public art pieces that fit the theme. Art must follow guidelines or it may be turned away.

segments.title: History: the 1986 Baker Beach effigy and move to the desert
segments.summary: Larry Harvey and friends burned an eight-foot wooden man on Baker Beach in San Francisco in 1986, inspired by a woman who had burned effigies there. The event grew, San Francisco objected, and the group moved the burning to the desert, with the Cacophony Society newsletter helping draw attendees. The hosts note it was not a reference to The Wicker Man.

segments.title: Temporary autonomous zone, BLM relationship, and no-commerce ethos
segments.summary: The festival moved fully to the desert in 1990 and is described as a temporary autonomous zone left largely alone by authorities; the organization works with the Bureau of Land Management. It is meant to be a gift-based culture without consumerism or commodification, with few paid costs beyond ice.

segments.title: CNN sponsor message
segments.summary: Advertisement for CNN's Morgan Spurlock: Inside Man series.

segments.title: Growth, ticket sales, and pricing
segments.summary: Attendance grew from hundreds to tens of thousands, with a cap now at around 50,000 and tickets selling out, first in 2011. Ticket policies limit scalping and use a sliding price scale where early buyers pay more; low-income tickets are offered, and scalpers sometimes sell below face value. Tickets are needed to attend.

segments.title: Ten principles, the Man statue, and the Burning Man philosophy
segments.summary: The ten principles became official in 2004 and include leave no trace, radical self-expression, radical inclusion, radical self-reliance, gifting, civic responsibility, participation, and immediacy. The city is laid out in a circle around the Man statue, around 100 feet tall, and this year's pavilion is designed like a flying saucer. The organization's website hopes to attract aliens and stimulate the economy. Hosts discuss the idea of bringing the attitude back home, and the economics-driven culture described in an interview about the confidence economy.

segments.title: Practical survival tips and safety concerns
segments.summary: Advice on water (a gallon per day per person plus more for bathing), sunscreen covered by dust, cold desert nights, bringing lights, rebar in art installations, fire-pit rules, bikes as the main transport since driving on the playa is not allowed, and adaptability. The hosts discuss adult-oriented camps, families attending, reports of sexual assaults, and the need to understand what you are getting into; a week-long stay isn't required.

segments.title: Source Family cult and Polyphonic Spree sidebar
segments.summary: Hosts discuss the documentary on the Source Family, a 1970s cult in Los Angeles that moved to Hawaii, and compare cults of that era. They mention the Source Family's band and the Polyphonic Spree, and a friend, Toby, who was in the Spree and produced a film.

segments.title: Burning the Man and organizational money disputes
segments.summary: Hosts note the Man is burned on the last night, reflect on the symbolism, and touch on reported disputes over money and board transfers between founders, including Jerry James, and the organization's large ticket revenue.

segments.title: Listener mail: correction on FDA blood donation ban
segments.summary: A listener (Cat) corrects an earlier episode: the American Red Cross does not set the policy that bars men who have sex with men from donating blood; the FDA does, and the Red Cross is legally bound by it and seeks change.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listener feedback through social media, email, and the website, and close the episode.
